How well do dogs eat on their first day in quarantine?

How likely are dogs to eat in the first 24 hours after arriving at a Quarantine Facilty?

Imagine being put in a box, and then on a plane, for an undetermined amount of time and then suddenly you are in a new place with strange people. Would you still have an appetite?

Cat in a box

This data is looking at whether or not a dog eats within 24 hours of arrival, and what sort of food is being offered.

Are smaller dogs as fussy as they say?

Boxplot comparing dog weights based on whether the dogs had eaten within the first 24 hours after arriving at the quarantine facility. The x-axis contains the categories “No” and “Yes”. The y-axis shows dog weight in kilograms. Dogs in the “Yes” category generally show a wider spread of weights compared to the “No” category. The median weight for dogs that ate appears slightly higher than for dogs that did not eat. Green boxes represent dogs that ate, while orange boxes represent dogs that did not eat.

The above graph is looking at the distribution of dog weights based on whether the dog has eaten within the first 24 hours being at a quarantine facility. The median line inside this box plot shows the middle weight value of each of the groups, and from this graph we can see that of the dogs that did not eat within the first 24 hours, their weights tended to be on the smaller side compared to those that did. However, the dogs that did not eat within the first 24 hours did also have a wider spread, whilst those that did had more consistent weights. Maybe smaller dogs are more likely to be fussy after all, or just more susceptible of stress being in an unfamiliar environment.

Do Owners know their pets palate best?

The above graph looks at how a dogs eating behaviour may differ based on the type of food being provided. It shows us that most dogs are recorded as having eaten within the first 24 hours (yes), with a much higher number of dogs being fed Royal Canin. This suggests that dogs given Royal Canin were more likely to have eaten within the first 24 hours compared to those given food by their owners. However, those given food by their owners shows a smaller total number of dogs overall. This would make it more susceptible to change when a dog does not eat it, as shown by the difference between ‘Yes’ and ‘No’ being less pronounced than for those fed Royal Canin. The number of dogs not eaten within 24 hours is relatively low across both food types, only more visible in the Royal Canin group due to its larger sample size. This does suggest that dogs are more likely to eat food their owner provided than not, so maybe their owner does know what they like after all.

Does Weight Matter?

The above graph shows how individual dog weights vary across different days in 2026. Each point represents a single recorded dogs weight on a specific day, in this instance their arrival. The results show that dog weights fluctuate across time, with no strong trend over time. The first recorded day has a much wider spread of weights, but also a fair few more observations. The other two days have fewer observations, yet sime more clustered values which suggests more consistent weight recordings. It does appear that dog weights remain relatively stable across time, and that any variation is more dependent on individual dogs rather than the date they arrived. It does show that the first recorded day was a lot busier than the remaining two days, and had some dogs with higher weights, but it is certainly not a consistent trend.
